bets.text: Doing the multiply-accumulate digitally inside SRAM keeps the density benefit of in-memory computing while giving bit-exact, repeatable results that analog arrays cannot.
INT8 operands with wide (INT32) accumulation are enough to match floating-point accuracy after post-training quantisation, so customers need not retrain.

Four identical, self-sufficient cores on one chip let the same silicon trade throughput, latency and multi-network operation, and scale further by putting several chips on a card (only the multi-chip part has independent support: about 4x from one to four chips).
A vision-first operator set and SDK is a sufficient first market for an edge accelerator.

generations.what_changed_from_previous: First product generation. The survey source mentions an earlier test chip, Thetis, taped out in December 2021; nothing else about it was found.

bets.text: A large on-chip L2 SRAM plus a very wide LPDDR5 interface removes the memory bottleneck for multi-user generative workloads on an in-memory-compute chip.
Putting RISC-V vector clusters and a video decoder on the accelerator moves pre- and post-processing off the host CPU and lowers system cost.
One SDK across generations protects customer software investment; a hand-programmable core language shortens the port of new model families.

generations.what_changed_from_previous: Second-generation AI cores, eight instead of Metis's four, each now paired with a large vector engine; added on-chip RISC-V vector clusters, 128 MB L2 SRAM, LPDDR5 in place of the LPDDR4X controller named for Metis, a video decoder and PCIe Gen4; manufactured on Samsung 5 nm per the foundry's quote. Target widened from computer vision to multi-modal and generative AI. The stated reasons are removing memory bottlenecks and reducing host CPU load. The independent evaluation's specification table additionally lists INT4/INT8/INT16 support, which the press release does not state.

bets.text: The digital in-memory core can be packaged as chiplets and scaled close to linearly from edge parts to cloud-class inference.

generations.what_changed_from_previous: Moves from a monolithic SoC to a chiplet-based design with proprietary RISC-V vector extensions and mixed precision; no source opened gives the reason beyond scaling from edge to cloud.
generations.next: Launch planned for 2028 according to the relayed announcement; not shipped as of the access date.

sources.author: Davide Baltieri, Tobia Peruzzi (Covision Lab, Bressanone, Italy)
sources.summary_en: Non-peer-reviewed arXiv white paper benchmarking ten edge inference accelerators on twelve reference models against an NVIDIA RTX A5000 running TensorRT. A single-chip Metis and a four-chip Metis PCIe card were physically measured (latency and frames per second for six convolutional models; four-chip scaling close to 4x). Six of the twelve models (the transformer ones, EfficientNet-B0, MobileNetV3-Small, ConvNeXt-Tiny, ResNeXt-101) did not run on Metis. Power was not measured; the power and TOPS/W figures in its tables are vendor specifications. Europa hardware was not available, so its row is vendor specification only (629 TOPS INT8, 45 W TDP, eight cores, 16 RISC-V vector units). The fetched text does not state batch size or whether the authors declare vendor independence.

sources.author: Axelera AI
sources.title_original: Metis: the best AI Processing Unit | Axelera AI
sources.summary_en: Vendor product page for the Metis AIPU. States peak compute at INT8, an energy-efficiency figure, typical power, a ResNet-50 throughput figure and a throughput-per-dollar figure, none with batch size, resolution or measurement method. Claims existing models run without retraining and that several Metis chips can be combined. Does not state process node, core count, the in-memory mechanism or on-chip memory.

sources.author: Axelera AI
sources.title_original: Axelera Announces Europa AIPU, Setting New Industry Benchmark for AI Accelerator Performance, Power Efficiency and Affordability
sources.summary_en: Vendor press release announcing Europa. Eight second-generation AI cores, each with digital in-memory compute and a large vector engine; two clusters of eight RISC-V vector cores for non-AI pre/post-processing; 128 MB on-chip L2 SRAM; a 256-bit LPDDR5 interface; hardware H.264/H.265 decode; PCIe Gen4 x4; 35x35 mm package; same Voyager SDK as Metis. A Samsung quote says the design is made on its 5 nm process. Targets multi-modal and generative AI plus vision from edge to enterprise server. Shipments of chip and PCIe card were planned for the first half of 2026. The efficiency comparison names no competitor, workload or method. No power figure is given. Card memory is described as single-chip 16 GB up to four-chip 256 GB. Calls Metis the first-generation product and lists integrators (Advantech, SECO) and testers.
quotes: 3 to 5 times performance efficiency (performance per watt and performance per dollar) over the leading industry solutions in the same product category

sources.author: Axelera AI team member (forum handle 'Spanner')
sources.summary_en: Vendor community announcement that Europa is shipping on two cards: Edge 232p (half-height half-length PCIe, one Europa) and Server 250p (full-height full-length, four Europa). Repeats the per-chip specification without power or precision. Introduces AxScript, a Python-embedded language for programming the AI cores directly, usable by hand or through an agent-assisted flow, alongside the existing automatic ONNX/PyTorch compiler; says the same code targets Metis and Europa and is meant to carry to Titania. Reports an internal port of a Qwen-family language model in one day. No ship date other than the post date; no public date for language-model support.

sources.author: Asif Ali Khan, Joao Paulo C. De Lima, Hamid Farzaneh, Jeronimo Castrillon (TU Dresden)
sources.title_original: The Landscape of Compute-near-memory and Compute-in-memory: A Research and Commercial Overview
sources.summary_en: arXiv survey preprint (no journal venue named on the page) with a commercial-landscape section. For Axelera it describes an SRAM-based digital in-memory compute engine, INT8 weights and activations with INT32 accumulation, a claim of FP32-level accuracy without retraining, an SoC of four AI cores plus a RISC-V control core, and a first test chip (Thetis) taped out in December 2021. Its only reference for these is the company website, so the content is a relay of vendor statements, not an independent inference. No node, TOPS or power given.

sources.author: Arteris, Inc. (press release via GlobeNewswire, mirrored by TipRanks)
sources.title_original: Arteris IP Licensed by Axelera AI to Accelerate Computer Vision at the Edge
sources.summary_en: Supplier press release. Metis has four identical AI cores, each able to run all layers of a standard network on its own; the cores can share one workload, run copies of one network, or run different networks. Cores, RISC-V controller, PCIe interface, LPDDR4X controller and security block are joined by a network-on-chip built with Arteris FlexWay. At that date Metis was on pre-order and with selected early-access customers. Says nothing about in-memory computing, TOPS or process.

sources.author: Maurizio Di Paolo Emilio (EE Times)
sources.title_original: Axelera AI Platform Accelerates Edge Application Deployment
sources.summary_en: Trade-press article built on vendor statements. Calls Metis the first-generation AIPU combining digital in-memory computing with RISC-V-controlled dataflow, says hardware and software had recently been delivered to customers with volume production as the next milestone, describes an M.2 module with one Metis and 512 MB LPDDR4x, and says the Voyager SDK covered computer-vision networks with language processing planned. Throughput and efficiency multiples are given against unnamed competitors with no benchmark. Links only to the vendor home page and two other EE Times pieces.

sources.author: Erik van Klinken (Techzine)
sources.title_original: Dutch startup Axelera AI raises over 60 million and unveils new chip
sources.summary_en: News item on the EUR 61.6 million EuroHPC DARE funding and the Titania announcement: a chiplet-based inference chip using the digital in-memory architecture with proprietary RISC-V vector extensions in a mixed-precision platform, for generative AI and vision, planned to launch in 2028. Adds only glossary-level explanation to the vendor announcement. Recorded because it is the only account of Titania opened in this session.
